entities.summary: Lê Trung Tông (983–1005) was the second emperor under the Early Lê dynasty. He held the throne for only three days in 1005. His reign was considered one of two shortest reigns in Vietnam's history, along with the reign of Dục Đức under the Nguyễn dynasty.

entities.name: Lê Trung Tông
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lê Trung Tông (983–1005), born Lê Long Việt, stands as a poignant, albeit brief, figure in the Early Lê dynasty of Đại Cồ Việt, a period defining Vietnamese independence from Chinese domination. His reign, lasting a mere three days in 1005, following the death of his father, Emperor Lê Đại Hành, highlights the brutal succession struggles and political instability that often characterized early medieval Vietnamese monarchies. His tragic demise at the hands of his half-brother, Lê Long Đĩnh, underscores a critical turning point that led to the dynasty's collapse and the subsequent rise of the Lý dynasty, shaping the foundational political landscape of independent Vietnam.

Born in 983 CE in Hoa Lư Ancient Capital, Lê Long Việt was the third son of Emperor Lê Đại Hành (Lê Hoàn), the founder of the Early Lê dynasty. Upon his father's death in 1005, Lê Long Việt, who had previously been recognized as Prince Nam Quốc Vương, was initially elevated to the throne. However, his ascension was immediately challenged by his ambitious and ruthless younger half-brother, Lê Long Đĩnh, the Prince of Khai Minh. The ensuing power struggle was swift and decisive; Lê Long Đĩnh orchestrated a coup, assassinating Lê Trung Tông after only three days as emperor, a duration that remains one of the shortest in Vietnamese imperial history, rivaled only by Dục Đức of the Nguyễn dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lê Trung Tông's extremely brief and violent reign in 1005, though minor in itself, served as a critical inflection point, precipitating the terminal decline of the Early Lê dynasty and directly facilitating the rise of the Lý dynasty, which shaped Vietnamese statehood for over two centuries.
